title: Eviction signature analysis + routed batching deep dive - Cobalt Biotech
summary: Deep technical session to trace recent cache degradations seen in prod: frequent evictions correlated with routed batch spikes and multi-tenant prefix collisions. Discussed data collection (eviction traces, per-prefix telemetry), short-term mitigations (pinning hot prefixes, reducing batch sizes), and long-term fixes (adaptive eviction heuristics, improved routing affinity). Action items include log capture, small-scale repro, and a follow-up benchmark in Redwood Dedicated or Private VPC.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-08 15:30 PDT
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Monica Li (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Voss (Cobalt CTO), Marco Reyes (Platform), Nina Park (ML Infra), Sam Okafor (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto): frequent KV evictions when batch routing switches and long contexts start to hit disk spill. Some telemetry gaps around per-prefix counters.

[00:00] Jamie Chen: ok, good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — we want to walk through the eviction signatures you captured, talk about how routed batching could be amplifying it, and propose capture and mitigations.

[00:28] Dr. Elena Voss: thanks jamie. to be clear, this is impacting a couple of our LLM endpoints — especially the patient-note generator where session context goes long, we see latency spikes and sometimes token drops.

[00:52] Marco Reyes: yeah. noticed a pattern — when traffic bursts from our downstream aggregator, batch routing sends a lot of heterogeneous requests to the same GPU set and then the KV layer starts spilling. we get evictions within a few seconds.

[01:15] Ravi Patel: when you say spills are you seeing disk paging or network RPC to remote KV?

[01:22] Marco Reyes: mostly local disk spill on the private deployment, but in a couple cases we saw remote fallback to Redis in our staging that made things worse. logs show "evict-prefix" events with two or three prefixes per session.

[01:41] Monica Li: can you share the eviction signature you mentioned earlier? the trace you sent had an odd interleaving of prefix ids.

[01:50] Nina Park: (shares link) yes, we attached the trace in the ticket. note: prefix ids are hashed with our tokenization overlay so names are scrambled, might be why some of your tooling couldn't correlate.

[02:10] Ravi Patel: looking at the trace, there are three clear signals: a) synchronized large batched windows arriving every ~120s b) prefix churn where small prefixes get re-populated quickly c) rapid KV TTL resets. that combination causes the local KV allocator to thrash.

[02:37] Jamie Chen: interesting — that TTL reset is something we occasionally see when clients re-stream full context instead of incremental appends. are you resending full session history on reconnects?

[02:46] Dr. Elena Voss: sometimes, yes. our frontend will rehydrate history on tab reload. we thought caching would handle it but seems to reset some internal prefixes.

[03:05] Sam Okafor: also wanted to flag our VPC egress constraints — any mitigation that requires heavy cross-host streaming is not acceptable; we prefer local fixes or a private deployment plan.

[03:18] Monica Li: noted. so we'll focus on host-local strategies first: reduce batch coalescing for heterogeneous traffic, increase prefix affinity so the same GPU keeps a given user's prefixes, and add short-term pin for known hot prefixes.

[04:02] Marco Reyes: pinning sounds good but are you concerned about long-term leak if many prefixes become hot?

[04:12] Ravi Patel: yes that's where eviction heuristics matter — we recommend adaptive eviction by hotness score and recency, not strict LRU. plus a circuit-breaker that rejects very large batch coalesces when cache saturation is detected.

[04:35] Dr. Elena Voss: what about quantization — we use 4-bit quantized variants in staging. can quantization affect eviction frequency?

[04:46] Jamie Chen: quantization changes memory footprint per KV entry, so yes — with aggressive quantization you can fit more keys per GPU, but the access patterns still determine churn. also vectorized kernel memory use can spike with long-token generation which pushes KV out.

[05:10] Nina Park: we saw spikes in GPU memory when sequence lengths exceeded 4k tokens, then the runtime decided to free KV aggressively. Is there a way to prioritize KV over intermediate activations?

[05:26] Ravi Patel: short answer: the runtime balances both, but we can tune the kernel scheduling to favor KV cache retention for pinned prefixes; that is a non-default optimization though. needs a small config change or a dedicated capacity profile.

[06:00] Jamie Chen: let's go through the telemetry we'll need. ideally: per-prefix hit/miss counters, eviction reason tags (ttl, memory-pressure, manual), batch composition metadata (homogeneous vs hetero), and per-batch route id. Marco — can you collect 48 hours of that?

[06:19] Marco Reyes: yes, we can try. how heavy is that telemetry? we worry about added overhead on the nodes.

[06:25] Monica Li: low to medium. counters are cheap; full stack traces every eviction are heavier. recommended: start with counters + sampled eviction traces (1 in 1000) for 48h. we also have a lightweight binary that can collect per-prefix histograms with sub-ms overhead.

[07:02] Sam Okafor: if we sample 1 in 1000 and we have millions of requests, that's still a lot. can you narrow sampling to the GPU groups that show thrash?

[07:12] Ravi Patel: yes, we'll provide a capture recipe: selector by route id + GPU shard id + time windows during bursts. that reduces noise.

[07:40] Dr. Elena Voss: can you explain more about routed batching? we thought batches are created per-GPU based on arrival window, how would routing change that?

[07:58] Ravi Patel: good question. Redwood's router has policies: latency-first, cost-first, and affinity. In your case, because of multi-tenant traffic, the router switched to a cost-first policy when one zone hit higher load, which coalesced heterogeneous requests onto fewer pools and increased prefix collisions. In short: routing created larger, mixed batches which is worse for KV locality.

[08:32] Marco Reyes: that matches our timeline — the bursts coincide with cross-region aggregator rebalancing.

[08:40] Monica Li: mitigation: enforce affinity on those critical routes or create a dedicated pool for patient-note endpoints so prefixes don't collide with other workloads. Dedicated capacity also lets us pin GPUs with larger local KV budgets.

[09:05] Dr. Elena Voss: dedicated capacity is interesting, but cost is a concern. what's the typical uplift to avoid this class of issue?

[09:14] Jamie Chen: typically 20-40% higher cost vs pure hosted because you reserve memory and GPU for consistent KV retention; but it's a predictable uplift. we can run a short benchmark to show token cost vs error/latency reduction.

[09:36] Nina Park: ok. on security — we run in a VPC with strict KMS policies. any Private deployment require local KMS integration?

[09:46] Ravi Patel: yes for Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM; no keys leave your control. We'll send the security pack. For dedicated hosted we can also provide customer-managed KMS proxies.

[10:10] Sam Okafor: wanted to call out data residency — some sessions have PHI. we need SOC2 plus audit trail for eviction and access. do you log who touched which prefix?

[10:20] Monica Li: we can surface audit logs for prefix access and eviction events with user identities mapped to JWT subject or service id. that will be part of the capture.

[10:45] Jamie Chen: next let's sketch a repro plan and quick mitigations. short-term: 1) reduce max coalescing window for affected routes, 2) pin 5-10 hot prefixes per user for 30 minutes, 3) increase per-GPU KV soft limit by 15% for a trial, 4) add sampling capture as discussed.

[11:10] Marco Reyes: we can try 1 and 4 immediately. pinning and increasing soft-limits we'll need a maintenance window.

[11:28] Ravi Patel: great. long-term: a) adaptive eviction with hotness scoring and prefix affinity b) router changes to avoid large heterogeneous batches during known bursts c) improved telemetry and tooling to surface prefix collision heatmaps.

[11:55] Dr. Elena Voss: how quickly can we get a small repro? we can sc simulate arrival patterns with a load driver.

[12:05] Monica Li: we have a load recipe; we'll share it. 30 minutes of scaled-up requests that mimic your aggregator should reproduce the thrash in staging.

[12:30] Nina Park: also note tokenization: we do some pre-token filters that can change prefix hashes when punctuation normalization shifts; might be causing false collisions. we should capture raw and normalized tokens for a subset.

[12:52] Ravi Patel: good catch — tokenization drift is a known source of apparent prefix collisions. include that in sampling.

[13:15] Jamie Chen: any blockers to collecting telemetry?

[13:20] Marco Reyes: need approval from security for sampled traces — will raise a ticket, ETA by Friday.

[13:28] Dr. Elena Voss: timeline constraints: we aim to have the patient-note endpoint stable within 3 weeks; a pilot on Dedicated or Private after we validate the mitigations.

[13:40] Ravi Patel: sounds reasonable. we'll prioritize the capture and a short-stage run.

[14:00] Monica Li: last thing — quantization interplay: if you move to an 8-bit activations profile, memory for activations goes down but inference latency can slightly increase; there is often a sweet spot. We'll propose a quantization/throughput matrix in the follow-up.

[14:20] Dr. Elena Voss: ok. thank you — that helps a lot.

Recap / Next steps in call:
- Redwood to provide capture recipe + load driver + sample config for reduced coalescing and pinning.
- Cobalt to enable sampled telemetry for two GPU shards and run 48h capture (selector by route id).
- Cobalt security to approve sampled traces by Friday.
- Redwood to schedule small repro run in staging and then a follow-up benchmark (15-30 mins) for Dedicated vs Hosted trade-offs.

[End of transcript]
